gap: No result ChatGPT got states a measured figure for the power station's own drain: The Technology Man measured the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 losing 20% of its charge in 12 hours with the AC inverter on and nothing plugged in (about 17 W). With only the DC side on, the charge stayed at 100%. Over an 8-hour workday that inverter drain adds about 136 Wh to a Starlink Mini plus MacBook Air load of about 320 Wh, and the measured draws (Mini about 21 W, MacBook Air M4 8.7 to 29.9 W) are well below the 450 Wh a day ChatGPT planned for.
standout_why: I opened starsurf.com's Starlink Mini power station guide. It has no measurement by a named reviewer or lab: the Mini figures (25–40 W) come from Starlink's spec sheet, it says nothing about MacBook draw, and it works out usable capacity with an unattributed 0.85 factor. ChatGPT's answers also used 25–40 W for the Mini and an assumed 85% usable capacity, called them estimates and not measured runtimes, and said only 'avoid leaving the AC inverter running' with no number attached. The cited Starlink Help Center pages give rated supply needs (a 100 W USB-C PD source), not measured draw, and they rendered empty when I fetched them. The Verge pages could not be fetched. Among the results ChatGPT got, none gives a measured inverter idle draw, a measured DC-side usable capacity, or a measured MacBook draw.
decides: The measurements support powering everything from DC and USB-C and switching the inverter off. Measured usable capacities in the 1 kWh class sit close together (Anker C1000 Gen 2: 850–907 Wh on AC and 844 Wh on DC; Jackery 1000 v2: 910 Wh; BLUETTI AC180: 950–983 Wh; EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus: 910 Wh). The inverter idle drain (about 14–17 W) changes the result more than which station you buy. On DC, 844 Wh ÷ about 320 Wh a day is about 2.6 workdays for the Anker C1000 Gen 2. Running through the inverter adds about 136 Wh a day, so roughly 850 ÷ 456 is about 1.9 days, which happens to be ChatGPT's own figure. That favours a station with two 100 W+ USB-C ports, such as the Anker C1000 Gen 2 (2× 140 W, per our page) or the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 (2× 100 W), so the Mini and the MacBook both avoid the inverter. The AC180 has only one 100 W USB-C port (per our page), so the second device would have to go through AC or 12 V. For multiple days, StorageReview measured 1.91 kWh out of the Elite 200 V2, about 6 workdays at 320 Wh by the same arithmetic.
